results.content: # Internal Standards in LC−MS Bioanalysis: Which, When, and How. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), **as a key platform in bioanalysis, can quantify analyte concentration in complex biological matrices**. For complex sample preparation processes (e.g., antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) quantification via surrogate peptides), the internal standard should be added early (e.g., before immunocapture) to track analyte behavior throughout the process. Currently, there is no clear-cut guideline regarding IS concentration, and several factors must be considered, including cross-interference between the internal standard and analyte, mass spectrometric sensitivity, and matrix effects. This range is expected to encompass the average peak concentration (Cmax) of most drugs and metabolites; therefore, it is recommended that the signal response of the internal standard be approximately 1/3 or 1/2 of the ULOQ of the analyte[11]. 13C labelled internal standards-A solution to minimize ion suppression effects in liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry analysis of drugs in biological samples.

Title: LC-MS/MS method for quantitation of gemcitabine and its metabolite 2′,2′-difluoro-2′-deoxyuridine in mouse plasma and brain tissue: Application to a preclinical pharmacokinetic study - ScienceDirect
# LC-MS/MS method for quantitation of gemcitabine and its metabolite 2′,2′-difluoro-2′-deoxyuridine in mouse plasma and brain tissue: Application to a preclinical pharmacokinetic study. A simple, fast, and robust method was developed and validated to measure dFdC and dFdU in mouse plasma and brain tissue. A simple, sensitive, and relatively fast assay was developed and validated for the quantitation of gemcitabine (dFdC) and its major metabolite 2**′**,2**′**-difluoro-2**′**-deoxyuridine (dFdU) in mouse plasma and brain tissue. We successfully applied the validated method to the analysis of dFdC and dFdU in mouse plasma, brain, and brain tumor tissue in a preclinical pharmacokinetic study. Due to the limitations of obtaining primary brain tumor tissue, it is important to use accurate murine models as a surrogate and develop methods to detect dFdC and its metabolite, 2**′**,2**′**-difluoro-2**′**-deoxyuridine (dFdU, Fig. 1) in both plasma, brain, and brain tumor tissues. Therefore, the objectives of the present study were to develop and validate a specific and sensitive LC MS/MS method to measure gemcitabine and dFdU in mouse plasma, brain tissue, and brain tumor tissue, and then use the method in a preclinical pharmacokinetic study. In this study, we developed and validated the simultaneous quantitation of dFdC and dFdU in mouse plasma and brain homogenate by LC–MS/MS. Protein precipitation followed by simple dilution was utilized to extract both analytes from a small sample (mouse plasma: 25 μL and mouse brain/brain tumor: 5 mg). ### Development of a sensitive and selective LC-MS/MS method for simultaneous determination of gemcitabine and 2,2-difluoro-2-deoxyuridine in human plasma. ### Determination of gemcitabine and its metabolite in extracellular fluid of rat brain tumor by ultra performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry using microdialysis sampling after intralesional chemotherapy. * ### Development and optimization of a high-throughput HPLC-MS/MS method for the simultaneous determination of Cedazuridine, Gemcitabine and its metabolite in mouse plasma. To investigate the effect of CDZ on the bioavailability and metabolism of GEM after oral administration, an HPLC-MS/MS method was developed for the simultaneous determination of CDZ, GEM, and its metabolite dFdU in mouse plasma. * ### Quantitative UHPLC–MS/MS Analysis of Gemcitabine and Its Active and Inactive Metabolites in Pig Plasma and Lung Tissue in Preparation of Locoregional Therapies for Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer.

Journal articles Metabolites MS (LC–MS/MS, HRMS, IMS). Reddy GN, Laltanpuii C, Sonti R | Bioanalysis, 13(22), 1697–1722 (2021) Keywords: biotransformation • LC–MS • metabolite profiling • plasma • urine Metabolite profiling is an indispensable part of drug discovery and development, enabling a comprehensive understanding of the drug's metabolic behavior. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry facilitates metabolite profiling by reducing sample complexity and providing high sensitivity. This review discusses the in vivo metabolite profiling involving LC-MS/MS and the utilization of QTOF, QQQ mass analyzers with a particular emphasis on a mass filter. Further, a summary of sample extraction procedures in biological matrices such as plasma, urine, feces, serum and hair as in vivo samples are outlined. ## To view this content, please register now for access. ## Related articles.
